title: Omar Abdullah Launches Signature Campaign for J&K Statehood Restoration
excerpt: The Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister used his Independence Day address to announce an eight-week door-to-door campaign across all 90 assembly constituencies, pushing back against linking statehood to terror attacks.
body:
• CM Omar Abdullah announced an eight-week, door-to-door signature campaign across all 90 assembly constituencies demanding restoration of J&K's statehood
  • Abdullah rejected linking statehood to the Pahalgam terror attack, saying the region's status should not be decided by "killers" or their handlers across the border
  • The Supreme Court has given the central government eight weeks to respond to the statehood restoration petition
  • Abdullah described the current Union Territory governance model as "a horse with its front legs tied" — built for failure, not success

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah used his Independence Day address at Bakshi Stadium in Srinagar to announce an intensive eight-week campaign to mobilize public support for restoring the region's statehood. Speaking at the ceremonial parade where he hoisted the Tricolour — the first elected chief minister to do so in years — Abdullah laid out a direct plan to take the statehood fight to every household in the Union Territory.

A Signature Campaign Across 90 Constituencies

Abdullah said he and his National Conference colleagues would fan out across all 90 assembly constituencies, going door to door to collect signatures and thumb impressions from citizens supporting the demand for statehood. The collected signatures would be submitted to both the central government and the Supreme Court.

https://x.com/GreaterKashmir/status/2088515261100085441

"We will move from place to place in all the 90 Assembly constituencies and knock at every door to obtain signatures and thumb impressions from those who cannot sign, seeking restoration of statehood."

— Omar Abdullah, Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir

The campaign follows a Supreme Court hearing that gave the Government of India eight weeks to file its response to the statehood restoration petition. Abdullah framed the campaign as a shift from written appeals and private meetings to direct public mobilization.

Rejecting the Terror-Statehood Linkage

The chief minister pushed back sharply against the Supreme Court's observation that "incidents like Pahalgam" — referring to the April attack that killed 26 civilians, mostly tourists, in the Baisaran meadow — must be considered when deciding on restoring statehood.

Abdullah called the linkage unjust, arguing that J&K's residents should not be punished for crimes committed by outsiders. He noted that citizens across the region, from Kathua to Kupwara, condemned the Pahalgam attack without prompting. Historically, he argued, elected governments had reduced militancy more effectively than alternative governance arrangements.

"Whether J&K gets statehood or not must be decided by the democracy of India and not by the killers of Pahalgam or their masters across the border in our neighbouring country."

— Omar Abdullah, Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir

A System Built for Failure

In one of the sharpest critiques of the Union Territory governance model, Abdullah likened it to "a horse with its front legs tied" — a system designed not for success but for failure. He disclosed that his government's cabinet decisions were being altered, blocked, or left to gather dust at the Raj Bhavan without approval.

Abdullah reflected on the political transformation since he last addressed an Independence Day function as the head of a state. Back then, J&K had its own identity, constitution, flag, and statehood. Since the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019 and the region's reorganization into a Union Territory, all of that had been stripped away.

He accused the bureaucracy of undermining elected authority, breaking what he called the "triple chain of accountability" linking the government, legislature, and people. The dual power structure, he argued, renders the elected government ineffective.

Fading Hopes but No Surrender

Abdullah acknowledged that his optimism about statehood was beginning to fade. He revealed that he had been repeatedly told that "documents are ready" and that an announcement was imminent — but nothing materialized.

The chief minister said he had paid a political price for trusting India's democratic institutions and the central government to restore J&K's rights, rather than taking a confrontational approach.

Despite the frustration, Abdullah presented a 10-month progress report of his government's work in education, health, social welfare, transport, tourism, and agriculture — areas where the administration had focused on maximizing the limited powers available to it.

The campaign is being seen as one of the most direct political mobilizations in the Kashmir Valley since the abrogation of Article 370 — a grassroots push to demonstrate that the demand for statehood carries an overwhelming popular mandate.
